BREAKING: Since the start of 2025, US jobs numbers have now been revised down in 16 out of 20 months by a total of -793,000 jobs.

This means that, on average, -39,650 jobs have been revised out of previously reported data each month during this period.

The most recent August and July jobs numbers were revised down by a total of -60,000.

Revisions to nonfarm payrolls have consistently occurred since the start of 2023.

If we apply this average to the +29,000 jobs add in September's report, it would imply a -10,650 contraction in nonfarm payrolls last month.

This would also mark their 3rd monthly decline of 2026, following a -156,000 drop in February and -10,000 in July.

What is happening here?

The Fed is in a bind because the markets are demanding rate hikes, but those hikes will have a disparate impact on borrowers. The Government cares about rising rates but they can always kick the can down the road (if markets let them). But homebuyers and weak credits don’t have that luxury. The hyperscalers could care less, since their returns on the debt that they issue are so outsized relative to what the Fed is charging for money. The Fed has one blunt instrument for many different constituents. But the message from the market is clear: the Fed should not have eased in 2025 and now must take those rate cuts back.

Executives in the Financials sector are turning cautious:

The unique seller/buyer ratio for Financials stood at 2.10x above its long-term average in Q3 2026, the highest reading across all major sectors.

This ratio compares the number of individual insiders who sold shares with the number who bought, regardless of how many times they sold.

The number of financial executives buying their own stocks in the sector fell to its lowest level in almost 23 years, while the number of sellers was not unusually high.

Energy and Technology followed, with ratios of 1.30x and 1.24x, respectively.

At the same time, the broader market seller/buyer ratio stood at 1.20x its long-term average last quarter, or 20% above the historical norm.

On the other hand, Consumer Staples had the lowest reading at just 0.50x, followed by Utilities at 0.55x and Materials at 0.57x.

Insider confidence is fading across key market sectors.

"That's how delusional these Bitcoiners are. He found something that was counter to all his work, and he decided to turn the findings upside down to fit his narrative"

This hilariously off base.

This finding was not "counter"  to my work... it's at the literal CORE of my work.

Bitcoin is unflinching.

It just keeps spitting out block after block every ~10 minutes.

But the human psychology around this thing is constantly shifting and evolving.

The crowd often gets too bullish and too bearish at the wrong times. So it's incredibly useful to see where people are at emotionally. It can give us a more holistic understanding of the Bitcoin market.

Understanding this better can help us weather volatility. Bitcoin can be damn hard to HODL when price is down and it seems like no one wants Bitcoin anymore.

But here's the thing.

This is exactly the most bullish time to buy.

I could obviously be wrong, we could have some news break and Bitcoin tanks.

This is always on the table.

But buying Bitcoin (a narrative/psychologically driven asset) when moods are historically low seems like a layup IMO.

Time will tell which of us is right.

Y'all know which side I'm on.

The employment downturn in the US Information sector is intensifying:

Information employment fell another -10,000 jobs in September, to 2.739 million, the lowest since December 2020.

Excluding the 2020 pandemic drop, this is the lowest level since December 2014.

In total, the Information industry has shed -376,000 jobs, or -12.1%, since the November 2022 peak.

To put this into perspective, during the 2001 recession and its aftermath, Information employment fell -568,000 jobs, or -15.3%, from March 2001 to December 2003.

The Information sector is losing jobs at a crisis pace.

BREAKING: Short interest in the Russell 2000 index is up to 8.0% of shares outstanding, the highest since at least 2019.

Since the start of 2025, this percentage has nearly doubled.

By comparison, before the 2022 bear market, short interest in small-cap stocks was ~3.5%.

This comes after the S&P 500 outperformed the Russell 2000 in Q3 2026 by 9.6 percentage points, its largest outperformance since Q1 2020.

Meanwhile, short interest in the S&P 500 ETF, $SPY, stands at ~9.0% of shares outstanding, below the 10.0% average seen in 2024-2025 and far below the 15.0% average between 2020 and 2023.

Are small caps set for a short squeeze?
